lead: Any VR, AR or MR experience is judged on three things: immersion, interaction and imagination. The three I's give a simple checklist for designers and examiners. Immersion asks how completely the system surrounds your senses and blocks out the real world. Interaction asks whether you can act and get a timely reply. Imagination asks whether the virtual world offers a scenario worth entering and rules you can learn. A weakness in one I spoils the whole experience. The three I's appear in product reviews, usability tests and the first unit of many VR courses.
prereq: You need: 1.1 for VR and virtual environment.

sections.h3: Immersion: the system's push into the world

blocks.text: Immersion is the degree to which the hardware and software wrap the user in the virtual world. It is a property of the system, not a feeling. It has two parts. Sensory immersion comes from the display and the sound system. Mental immersion comes from the story, the task and your engagement.

Sensory immersion depends on measurable system properties: field of view, stereo display, resolution, frame rate, latency, spatial sound and haptics. A wide field of view covers more of your eye. Stereo gives each eye a slightly different image. High resolution and frame rate keep the image sharp and steady. Low latency keeps the image in step with your head. Spatial sound places a voice at your left ear. Haptics adds touch and force.

Mental immersion depends on content: a clear goal, a believable world, and a task that holds attention. A simple game with a strong task can immerse more than a photorealistic scene with nothing to do.

Keep two words apart. Immersion is a property of the system. Presence is the user's feeling of 'being there'. A system can be highly immersive by design, yet a tired user may feel little presence. Immersion helps presence, but the two are not the same word.

sections.h3: Interaction: the loop that must keep time

blocks.text: Interaction is the two-way exchange between the user and the system. The system reads input from the user and returns feedback. Input includes head tracking, hand tracking, data gloves, voice and controllers. Feedback includes image, sound and force.

Real-time response is the hard requirement. Head tracking that lags by more than about 20 ms between your motion and the matching image causes discomfort. The world arrives late. Your eyes see one position; your inner ear reports another. The conflict can cause dizziness, headache and nausea.

Interaction quality is not only speed. The mapping must feel natural. Turning your head should turn the view by the same angle. Reaching for a virtual switch should move the virtual hand by the same distance. Feedback must match the action: a virtual ball should sound like a ball when it hits a wall.

items: Head tracking: reads the orientation and position of the head.
Hand tracking or gloves: read finger and hand pose.
Controllers: read buttons, triggers and sticks.

sections.h3: Imagination: the content and the mental model

blocks.text: Imagination is the designer's content and the user's mental model. The designer chooses the scenario, the rules and the difficulty. The user builds a mental model of what the world allows. A flight simulator lets you fly a plane without fuel cost or risk. A molecular viewer lets you walk through a molecule. A surgical trainer lets you rehearse a cut before you touch a patient.

Imagination is not only fantasy. It is the ability to do something that real life forbids: shrink to the size of a cell, pause a chemical reaction, repeat a dangerous procedure ten times. The rules must be clear. If the world breaks its own rules, the mental model fails and the other two I's cannot save the experience.

Some syllabi write the three I's as immersion, interaction and information. In most VR texts the third is imagination. Information is part of the content, but it is too narrow: imagination covers scenario, rules and the user's mental model.

examples.question: A surgical trainer gives the trainee a headset with a 110° field of view and stereo sound, a tracked glove on each hand, and a virtual patient that bleeds when cut. (a) Name the three I's in this system. (b) The head-tracking lag is measured at 100 ms. The discomfort threshold is about 20 ms. Which I fails first, and what does the user feel? Give the excess lag and the ratio.
steps: Immersion: the 110° field of view, the stereo headset display, and the stereo sound are sensory system properties.
Interaction: the tracked gloves read hand motion, and a cut returns visible bleeding and sound. This is the input-feedback loop.
Imagination: the surgical scenario, the tissue rules, and rehearsal without a live patient are content and mental model.
Lag check: measured lag = 100 ms; limit = 20 ms; excess = 100 − 20 = 80 ms; ratio = 100 ÷ 20 = 5.

Failure order: interaction fails first. The image arrives 100 ms after the head motion. The eyes see one position while the inner ear reports another. This sensory conflict causes dizziness and loss of presence.
examples.answer: Immersion is the 110° stereo view and stereo sound; interaction is the tracked gloves plus bleeding and sound feedback; imagination is the surgical scenario. Interaction fails first: 100 ms exceeds the 20 ms limit by 80 ms (5 times), causing dizziness and loss of presence.
examples.check:
lag = 100
limit = 20
excess = lag - limit
ratio = lag / limit
print(excess)
print(ratio)

traps: Writing immersion = good graphics. Field of view and latency matter more than polygon count.
Using immersion and presence as synonyms. Immersion is a system property; presence is the user's feeling.
Forgetting that mental immersion is not a display property. Story and task can immerse with simple graphics.
Missing the real-time limit. Head-tracking lag above about 20 ms causes discomfort, no matter how good the content.
Assuming the third I is always information. Most VR texts use imagination; information is a narrower reading.

quiz.q: Define immersion and presence. State one difference between them.
quiz.a: Immersion is the degree to which the system surrounds the user's senses with the virtual world; it is a property of the system. Presence is the user's feeling of being there. Difference: immersion belongs to the system, presence belongs to the user.

quiz.q: List four input devices and three feedback channels used in VR interaction.
quiz.a: Inputs: head tracking, hand tracking, data gloves, voice, controllers. Feedback: image, sound, force.

quiz.q: Why does head-tracking lag above about 20 ms cause discomfort?
quiz.a: The image arrives after the head motion. The eyes see one position while the inner ear reports another. This sensory conflict can cause dizziness, headache and nausea.

quiz.q: A headset has 90° field of view and 60 ms head-tracking lag. Which I is weakest? Give the excess over the 20 ms limit.
quiz.a: Interaction is weakest because 60 ms is above the 20 ms limit. Excess = 60 − 20 = 40 ms.

quiz.q: A photorealistic VR scene has no task and a 5 ms lag. Which I is weak, and why?
quiz.a: Mental immersion is weak, because there is no goal or task to hold attention, and imagination is weak, because the world offers no scenario or rules to build a mental model. Sensory immersion is high (photorealistic) and interaction is fast (5 ms lag).

quiz.q: Distinguish sensory immersion from mental immersion.
quiz.a: Sensory immersion comes from display and sound properties: field of view, stereo, resolution, frame rate, latency, spatial sound, haptics. Mental immersion comes from story, task and engagement.

quiz.q: Some syllabi call the third I 'information'. Why is imagination a better term?
quiz.a: Information is only content. Imagination also covers the scenario, the rules and the user's mental model. It explains why users can do things real life forbids, such as flying a plane or walking through a molecule.

quiz.q: A virtual chemistry lab lets students shrink to molecular scale and repeat an explosive reaction safely. Which I does this mainly illustrate?
quiz.a: Imagination, because the scenario and rules let users do something real life forbids.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industry UX teams often score the three I's separately in headset reviews and training simulators. Presence questionnaires and cybersickness scales are research tools built on the same split. Newer curricula add embodiment and social presence as extra lenses. Search for presence questionnaire, VR usability heuristics, and cybersickness latency if you want the measurement side.
